extracted.intended_audience: geologists, naturalists, and students of geology/paleontology (educated 19th-century scientific readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and criteria for classifying rocks, recognizing metamorphism and eruptive/contact phenomena, and determining relative ages of formations primarily via stratigraphic relations and fossil evidence. Emphasizes observable field signs (superposition, cross-cutting relations, fossil assemblages, mineralogical changes) and chemical/physical indicators of processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superposition principle for relative dating
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of succession, and the relative age of the different formations, may be recognized by the superposition of the sedimentary, metamorphic, and conglomerate strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vertical stacking (which strata overlie which) as a primary field criterion for relative age. This is presented as one of several means to determine relative chronology of formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of organic remains (palaeontological evidence) for chronometry
rubrics_metrics.description: With the greatest certainty [relative age] may be recognized by the presence of organic remains and the differences of their structure; the application of botanical and zoological evidence to determine the relative age of rocks is 'chronometry of the earth's surface.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paleontological investigations (comparing fossil floras and faunas) are emphasized as the most reliable method to determine relative ages and succession of strata. Index fossils and family-level changes through time are used to correlate and date formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cutting relations (traversing rocks are younger)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the traversing rocks must be of more recent origin than the traversed, we learn from the relations of stratification existing between the porphyry and the argentiferous ores ... that these formations are at any rate more recent than the vegetable remains found in carboniferous strata and in the red sandstone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the principle that intrusions, veins, or traversing masses are younger than the rocks they cut; use cross-cutting relationships to order events and relative ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineralogical and textural indicators of contact metamorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamorphism produced by massive eruptive rocks on compact calcareous beds is indicated by a formation without any trace of stratification or the fossil remains it once contained, consisting of a granular aggregation of crystals (e.g., dolomite). Cavities are covered with rhomboidal crystals, talc laminae scattered, traversed by serpentine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for loss of stratification and fossils, granular crystalline texture, new mineral growth (rhomboidal crystals of magnesian spar, talc laminae, serpentine) and sharp contacts adjacent to eruptive masses as evidence of metamorphism by igneous intrusion or Plutonic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic features of veins formed by sublimation/sublimate deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Veins formed by volcanic/plutonic vapors show arrangement of particles in layers parallel with vein margins, regular analogous layers on opposite walls, and elongated cellular cavities in the middle; these frequently afford direct evidence of the Plutonic process of sublimation in metalliferous veins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these characteristic micro- and macro-structures (layering parallel to vein margins, mirrored layering on both walls, central cellular cavities) to infer formation by vapor-driven sublimation and deposition from the interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact-mineral assemblages as indicators of eruptive influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Formation of garnets in argillaceous schist in contact with basalt and dolerite, and occurrence of various crystals (garnets, vesuvian, augite, ceylanite) on contact surfaces between erupted and sedimentary rock, indicate contact phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify characteristic minerals formed at contacts (e.g., garnet formation, specific crystal suites) to diagnose contact metamorphism and the nature of the intrusive rock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical transformation via vapors (e.g., limestone to gypsum)
rubrics_metrics.description: A third mode of transformation of carbonate of lime is ascribed to emission, in ancient periods, of vapors of sulphuric acid; transformation of limestone into gypsum is analogous to penetration by rock salt and sulphur deposited from sulphureted aqueous vapor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of vapor-phase chemical alteration (presence of gypsum, rock salt, sulphur deposits in fissures—even far from active volcanoes) when inferring non-contact chemical transformations of carbonates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and origin of conglomerates/detrital rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Conglomerates ('rocks of detritus') manifest characters of a double origin: mechanically accumulated fragments cemented by oxides or argillaceous/calcareous substances, but some are formed by friction/confinement when erupted rocks are propelled through fissures (friction 'conglomerates').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish detrital/conglomerate origins by grain shape (rounded or angular), cementing matrix, and context (marine/water deposition vs frictional emplacement around rising eruptive bodies). Examples: friction conglomerates abundant near eruptive intrusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineral composition as basis for rock classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances designated as 'rocks' are determinate associations of a small number of minerals (e.g., quartz, feldspar, and mica are principal constituents of granite); quantitative relations of minerals differ between rock types and define them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagnostic mineral assemblages and their proportions (e.g., relative amounts of alumina and silica) to classify rock types and infer petrogenesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of faunal/floral succession and assemblages for correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain species or families (e.g., Goniatites, Ceratites, Arietes) and larger faunal assemblages sometimes constitute whole formations; the association and succession of families and species permit dividing and correlating strata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ index fossils and family-level distributions (e.g., ammonite subgroups to particular formations) to correlate strata regionally and recognize stratigraphic levels within formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation mode informs type of biological information recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Different preservation (imprints, coprolites, ink bags, soft tissues) yield different information: imprints show behavior/tracks, coprolites indicate diet and digestive anatomy, preserved soft parts (ink bag, mantle, eyes) reveal anatomy and coloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the type of fossil preservation to determine what biological, ecological, or behavioral data can be inferred (e.g., coprolites → diet; ink bag → pigmentation; tracks → locomotion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing natural minerals from artificial analogues with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial production of minerals (in scoriae or by chemists) can yield crystals identical in composition and form to natural minerals, but differences (occurrence, associations) must be considered; distinguish scoriae accidentally formed from intentionally produced minerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experimental analogues as guides for interpreting natural mineral formation, but be cautious: laboratory or industrial products may replicate forms yet lack geologic context; do not over-interpret identity of processes solely from crystalline similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from recurring associations of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When two phenomena are always associated (e.g., occurrence of melaphyre and transformation of compact limestone), if the second occurs without the first in some places, the contradiction may be due to absence of some conditions attendant on the causes; repeated association justifies inference of a causal relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply probabilistic reasoning from consistent co-occurrence of features to infer causal relations, but remain open to exceptional cases where some necessary conditions are absent; do not reject general causal hypotheses because of isolated exceptions.
